Rule. Hold this rule for When to name a pattern: Say the force first, then the name, and decline the structure when a branch is enough. Say it before you pick a tool from Design patterns.

Why it matters. Interviewers on the Design patterns track listen for whether you can name the idea when to name a pattern and refuse the common wrong pick. The summary is the force: Say the force first, then the name, and decline the structure when a branch is enough. If you cannot restate it, you will drift into product names or trivia.

SAMPLE example. SAMPLE: a prompt lands that fits When to name a pattern. You restate the force in one sentence — Say the force first, then the name, and decline the structure when a branch is enough. — then show a tiny walkthrough that would fail if you ignored that force. You label the SAMPLE answer with the cost or the tradeoff, not with a brand name.

When to use. Use When to name a pattern when the prompt's access pattern or force matches the summary above, when a prior slug in its after-list is already in hand, and when saying the rule changes which next step you take.

When to refuse. Refuse When to name a pattern when a simpler tool already covers the force, when a prerequisite in after is still missing, or when applying it would invent a mechanism the track never taught. Prefer naming the missing slug over bluffing.
